How long is a coastline?

It depends on the ruler. Measure Britain with 200 km strides and you get one answer; with 10 km strides, a much bigger one — and the number never settles down. Pick an island, drag the divider, and watch a “fact” refuse to exist.

Ruler length

The Richardson plot

Shrink the ruler, grow the coast

In the 1950s Lewis Fry Richardson noticed that Spain and Portugal disagreed about the length of their shared border by hundreds of kilometres — each had simply walked it with a different ruler. Plotting measured length against ruler length on log–log axes, he found not convergence but a straight line: every halving of the ruler multiplies the length by a fixed factor.

Benoit Mandelbrot read the slope of that line as a fractal dimension D = 1 − slope. A tame curve has D near 1; the wilder the coast, the higher it climbs. Each curve on the right is one of the five islands, walked with some fifty different rulers.

Measured length vs. ruler length · log–log

Fractal dimension

A number that isn’t a length

Since “the” length of a coast doesn’t exist, D is the honest way to compare them: it measures how fast the length grows as the ruler shrinks. Sardinia’s Mediterranean shore barely budges; Spitsbergen’s glacier-carved fjords punish every smaller ruler.

Why it happens

Detail all the way down

A coastline is wiggly at every scale: gulfs contain bays, bays contain coves, coves contain boulders, boulders have crevices. A long ruler bridges straight over all of it; each shorter ruler is forced into wrinkles the previous one skipped, and every wrinkle adds length. Smooth curves run out of new detail — coastlines, over an enormous range of scales, don’t.

This is why published figures disagree so wildly. The CIA World Factbook lists the United Kingdom’s coastline at 12,429 km, while the Ordnance Survey’s high-water line of mainland Great Britain runs to roughly 17,820 km. Neither is wrong — they measured with different rulers. In this survey, Great Britain’s ring at full OpenStreetMap detail (907,738 surveyed points) comes to 14,567 km, and a finer survey would find more still.

Mandelbrot opened his 1967 paper on exactly this puzzle — How Long Is the Coast of Britain? — and the answer he gave made this island the founding example of fractal geometry.

Method

Coastline segments from the OSM coastlines-split-4326 extract were stitched into closed rings; the largest ring per region is shown, Douglas–Peucker-simplified from up to ~900k points to a web-friendly 25–60k. Lengths use the divider (compass-walking) method computed on the WGS84 sphere: from each anchor, the walk advances to the exact point one ruler-length away along the coast, great-circle. The Richardson fit uses the central portion of each curve; below ~1 km the simplified base data itself limits detail.
